 At a glance
 A regulation that sought to replace duration-of-status admissions with fixed terms for foreign students, exchange visitors and foreign media representatives has been vacated.  
 A federal district court in Massachusetts found that the regulation was contrary to Congress’s intent in creating the subject visa programs and violated the Administrative Procedure Act. The Trump Administration is expected to appeal.  
 The issue
 Today, a federal district court vacated the Department of Homeland Security regulation that sought to subject F, J, and I nonimmigrants to fixed periods of admission. Judge Dennis Saylor of the federal district court for the district of Massachusetts granted the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment and struck down the regulation, finding that the regulation exceeded DHS’s authority and was inconsistent with Congress’s intent in creating the affected visa programs. The case is  Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration et al. v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security et al. , 1:26-cv-13799 (D. Mass., filed Aug. 18, 2026). 
 In August, a coalition of educational organizations and unions – including NAFSA, the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the American Federation of Teachers, and the UAW – filed a  lawsuit  in the federal district court of Massachusetts, alleging that the  regulation  that sought to replace duration-of-status admissions with fixed admission periods for F-1 foreign students, J-1 exchange visitors, I representatives of foreign information media, and their dependents violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). In September, the court temporarily postponed the effective date of the rule while the litigation proceeded.  
 The Trump Administration is expected to appeal the ruling.
